name: Gilgamesh: The Life of a Poem
date: Princeton University Press, hardcover 24 September 2019 (ISBN 9780691195247, 192 pages); paperback ISBN 9780691205168; ebook ISBN 9780691196992. UK price 20 pounds.
creator: Michael Schmidt (b. 1947), British-based literary historian, poet, novelist and translator; founder of Carcanet Press and PN Review; Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature; OBE 2006; based in Manchester. Also author of The Novel: A Biography and The First Poets. As Carcanet's publisher he brought out Jenny Lewis's Gilgamesh Retold (2018), which the book discusses at length.
form: Critical essay and reception history (literary criticism), not a translation. A guided walk through the Standard Babylonian poem tablet by tablet, combined with an account of the text's rediscovery and fragmentary state, a comparative chapter ('How You Tell It') that sets many English versions of the same passage side by side, and a survey of modern poets' responses (Schmidt canvassed around fifty poets about their encounters with the poem).
translator_access: Schmidt does not read Akkadian or Sumerian and says so; he writes as a self-declared non-specialist. He relies chiefly on Andrew George's translations (Penguin 1999/2003 and the 2003 critical edition) and on Jenny Lewis's 2018 version, and quotes many other English versions for comparison. Thomas W. Hodgkinson (The Spectator, 12 October 2019) pointed out the irony: Schmidt is 'enjoyably scornful' of translations by people who cannot read the original languages, yet cannot read them himself.
scholarly_adviser: N/A as a translation. Schmidt's scholarly anchor is Andrew George, whose translation and 2003 critical edition he treats as the reference text. [uncertain: no formally named adviser found]
versions_used: Discusses the Standard Babylonian version attributed to Sin-leqi-unninni (who, Schmidt says, added 'prefatory lines … and a reprise that echoes the opening but in a darker tone'), the earlier Old Babylonian material (whose qualities, he notes, were partly lost in the standard version), and the separate Sumerian Gilgamesh poems. Stresses that there is 'no single canonical text for Gilgamesh as there is for the Iliad' and that the text keeps changing as new fragments surface. English versions discussed include R. Campbell Thompson (1928, hexameters), E. A. Speiser (ANET, 1955), N. K. Sandars (Penguin prose, 1960), Nigel Dennis, Herbert Mason, Stephanie Dalley (OUP 1989), David Ferry (1992), Andrew George (1999), Benjamin Foster (2001), Stephen Mitchell (2004), Yusef Komunyakaa (verse play, 2006), Edwin Morgan (theatre version), Philip Terry's Dictator (Globish adaptation) and Jenny Lewis (2018). [uncertain: whether the Sulaymaniyah tablet published in 2014 is discussed was not confirmed]
non_standard_material: As a critic Schmidt praises visible marking over silent merging. He singles out George's system of roman type for secure text, brackets for probable restorations and italics for plausible but unattested interpolations (quoted in David Gullette's Arts Fuse review), and faults versions that blend recensions or invent connective material without saying so. His complaint about Sandars is that she 'plays false with sequence' and cut the verbatim repetitions to make the poem easier for modern readers (Literary Review, December 2019).
gap_policy: Schmidt argues that the gaps should be shown, not smoothed over. He treats the fragmentary, multi-lingual state of the poem as a feature: 'We are not dealing with a single world and time. We are not dealing with a single language.' He tells readers to 'follow the scholar's route' and read versions with notes that reveal lacunae and ambiguities, and says George's versions are readable because they 'remain focused on what we have of the original and do not pretend to take independent flight.' Max Norman (LARB, December 2019) summarises the point: George's foreignizing version keeps gaps and brackets, forcing readers to meet the poem as a historical document as well as a story.
typography_of_absence: Discussed, not practised: Schmidt quotes George's page with its brackets, italics and ellipses as the honest model, and contrasts it with the seamless prose of Sandars and the continuous verse of the poets' 'retellings' (Mitchell, Ferry), where absence is invisible. His own quotations reproduce each translator's conventions. [uncertain: exact page examples not verified]
tablet_xii: Discussed as part of his tablet-by-tablet walk-through, which covers twelve tablets. None of the reviews examined report a distinctive argument about Tablet XII. Schmidt emphasises instead Sin-leqi-unninni's frame, where the closing reprise echoes the opening 'in a darker tone', which implies he reads the walls of Uruk at the end of Tablet XI as the poem's formal close. [uncertain]
turning_point: Schmidt refuses a single hinge because he refuses the frame of a unified epic. He asks whether the poem is 'the first road novel, the first trip to hell, the first Deluge, the first heterosexual romance in poetry?' and argues that 'Gilgamesh did not know it was "the first epic poem." It did not know it was an epic at all.' Within his walk-through, reviewers report that Enkidu's death is what 'precipitates the poem's final episodes' (David Cooke, Manchester Review), turning Gilgamesh from a wayward ruler into a seeker after wisdom through suffering. He also highlights Rilke's reading of the poem as 'das Epos der Todesfurcht' (the epic of the fear of death), which places the hinge at the moment mortality becomes personal. The formal hinge he stresses is the Standard Babylonian frame: a prologue and a reprise that 'echoes the opening but in a darker tone'. [uncertain: Schmidt's own statement of a single turning point not found]
arc_interpretation: Maturity through grief, but held loosely and kept plural. Schmidt reads the story as the education of a wayward king through friendship and loss (Rod Mengham, one of the poets he quotes, says the poem 'enshrines friendship as the bedrock of our negotiations with the world'), and pays attention to Humbaba as 'defender of his luxuriant, perfumed and peaceful kingdom', giving the cedar forest episode an ecological reading against the poem's urban setting. His larger claim is that the poem should not be read as a proto-Homeric epic with a coherent narrator: 'We will never penetrate to the subjectivity of the poem, the "I" of the narrator', which is 'an invention of the translator'. Joan Acocella (New Yorker, 7 October 2019) summarised his view that Gilgamesh is not a finished composition but 'something more like life, untidy, ambiguous'. Max Norman (LARB) describes Schmidt's framing of the poem as an agon, a contest that resists both translation and imitation.
key_passages: The book's central comparative chapter, 'How You Tell It', quotes version after version of Shamhat's seduction of Enkidu in Tablet I and shows how each translator's word choice, notation and form change the scene. The survey runs from R. Campbell Thompson's 1928 hexameters, with Shamhat's 'bosom' and 'comeliness' and archaic contractions like 'turn'd' and 'aye' that Schmidt finds unintentionally comic, through E. A. Speiser's 'varnished and prim' 1955 version with 'an instinct for cliché', to recent versions that are more anatomical and in which Shamhat takes the lead. He says some of these are 'worthy of the Bad Sex in Fiction Award, adding circumstantial detail'. Jenny Lewis's version is praised for giving Enkidu more agency and for wresting the poem 'from its usual male-gendered specificity'. On Sandars, he argues that her addition of a first-person narrator on the model of the Odyssey makes the Penguin version 'inadvertently colonial' (Spectator). Siduri's advice, the Tablet XI bedchamber lines and the closing walls of Uruk are covered in the tablet-by-tablet chapters, but reviews do not report a comparative treatment of them. [uncertain: whether passages other than Shamhat get side-by-side treatment]
diction_and_metre: Schmidt writes prose criticism, not verse. Reviewers describe the register as 'learned yet lively' (John Butler, Asian Review of Books), 'sure-footed in its scholarship but hip and occasionally hilarious in its tone' (David Gullette, Arts Fuse). As a critic of metre he mocks archaising hexameters (Campbell Thompson), dislikes the prim idiom of Speiser, and values Lewis's 'gapped or sprung phrasal line' as 'the most voice-friendly version since Edwin Morgan's theatre adaptation'.
sample_line: "Gilgamesh did not know it was 'the first epic poem.' It did not know it was an epic at all." (Schmidt, Gilgamesh: The Life of a Poem, 2019, quoted by John Butler, Asian Review of Books, 26 September 2019)
critical_response: Largely favourable. Joan Acocella, The New Yorker (7 October 2019): 'Schmidt's argument for the poem as poetry, in the modern sense, concrete, unglazed, tough on the mind, is touching and persuasive'; she read it 'spellbound, in one sitting'. James Romm, Wall Street Journal: 'freshly framed observations help renew one of the world's oldest surviving tales.' Publishers Weekly: 'An insightful, stimulating book sure to breathe new life into the would-be immortal king.' John Butler, Asian Review of Books (26 September 2019): 'If you have never read Gilgamesh before, Schmidt could be Virgil to your Dante.' David Cooke, The Manchester Review: 'stimulating, informative and elegantly written', hoped to become 'an indispensable guide for all future readers of Gilgamesh'. David Gullette, The Arts Fuse: 'wonderfully readable'. Max Norman, Los Angeles Review of Books (19 December 2019): praises the 'careful and self-reflexive approach'. Peter McDonald: 'a remarkable and hugely worthwhile book'. The main dissent is Thomas W. Hodgkinson, The Spectator (12 October 2019): 'as many oversights as insights', too much plot summary, and the omission of George Smith's discovery story from a book claiming to tell the poem's 'life'.
controversies: Two charges. First, consistency: Schmidt attacks 'languageless' translators (they 'drain the stream and harvest the fish by hand') and quotes Gabriel Josipovici that 'imitation as against informed translation is a license for laziness', yet he cannot read Akkadian either (Hodgkinson, Spectator). Second, conflict of interest: he publishes Jenny Lewis through Carcanet and gives her version prominent praise. Butler also notes his dismissal of epic-genre readings 'may raise some eyebrows, scholarly or otherwise'. No dispute over provenance or authorship.
regional_reception: Hodgkinson (Spectator) criticises the book's Western frame: its poets' responses come from British, American, Israeli and New Zealand writers but 'not, for some reason, from Iran, Iraq, Turkey or Syria', and it does not assess Arabic, Persian or Turkish translations. Norman (LARB) credits Schmidt with pointing toward a less imperialist approach to world literature, and Schmidt's own charge that Sandars is 'inadvertently colonial' shows he is aware of the issue. No Arabic or Kurdish translation of the book was found. [uncertain]
ai_craft_tension: Schmidt gives Lee a ready vocabulary for the machine versus human question without ever mentioning machines. He sorts versions by how honestly they show what is missing: George's brackets and italics on one side, the smooth prose of Sandars and the fluent retellings of poets without Akkadian on the other. That is the same split between a model's fluent output and a scholar's marked-up uncertainty. His line that the narrator's 'I' is 'an invention of the translator' fits generated text especially well: any coherent voice a machine gives Gilgamesh is supplied, not recovered. His 'How You Tell It' chapter works as a benchmark: one passage, many renderings, each revealing its era's taste (Campbell Thompson's 'bosom', Speiser's primness, the Bad Sex Award candidates). A model's rendering would be one more entry in that line-up, and Schmidt's test is whether it takes 'independent flight' or stays with 'what we have of the original'. What he says still needs a human is judgement about form and ethics: choosing to leave the gaps open, noticing a colonial frame, and hearing the 'static' when 'the volume refuses to be evenly controlled'.
essay_hooks: 1) 'Gilgamesh did not know it was "the first epic poem." It did not know it was an epic at all.' (quoted by Butler, Asian Review of Books). 2) 'We will never penetrate to the subjectivity of the poem, the "I" of the narrator', which is 'an invention of the translator' (same review). 3) Translators without the language 'drain the stream and harvest the fish by hand' (Schmidt, Literary Review, December 2019). 4) Some recent versions of the Shamhat scene are 'worthy of the Bad Sex in Fiction Award' (same). 5) Speiser's 1955 version is 'varnished and prim' with 'an instinct for cliché'; Campbell Thompson's 1928 hexameters give Shamhat a 'bosom' and 'comeliness'. 6) Sandars's million-selling Penguin is 'inadvertently colonial' because she gave the poem an Odyssey-style first-person narrator (Spectator). 7) George's versions work because they 'do not pretend to take independent flight'. 8) Is it 'the first road novel, the first trip to hell, the first Deluge, the first heterosexual romance in poetry?' 9) Irony: a critic who cannot read Akkadian scolding translators who cannot read Akkadian (Hodgkinson, Spectator), which mirrors any human reviewing a model's translation. 10) Rilke called it 'das Epos der Todesfurcht', the epic of the fear of death.
